title: Wet Floor & Spillage Management
blurb: How to deal with a spill properly: spot it, sign it, clean it, dry it, and report what keeps coming back.
siteNotes: Where wet floor signs, mops, absorbent and spill kits are kept
The correct clean-up method and kit for oil, grease and broken glass
Who to report recurring wet spots to on each shift
legalNotes: From BHB-10MT-32 (the venue's 10-minute trainer). Taught as written.

CHECK: the trainer says slips are "the most common accident in our industry". HSE reports slips and trips as the most common cause of major injury across all workplaces, but the hospitality claim is not verified here. The slides say "one of the biggest causes" only.
Keeping floors free of hazards and warning of wet floors: general duties under the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974; see also the slips-trips-falls session.

cards.title: Wet Floor & Spillage Management
cards.body:
By the end of this session you can:
- explain why a barely visible wet patch matters
- deal with a spill in four steps
- know when to report a spill that keeps coming back

cards.title: A wet patch you can barely see
cards.body: Wet floors are one of the biggest causes of slips. A wet patch you can barely see can put a guest or colleague flat on their back in an instant. The way we deal with spills says a lot about how safe our venue really is.

items.title: Hard to see
items.text: A thin wet patch is easy to miss.

items.title: Instant
items.text: One step is all it takes.

items.title: Our standard
items.text: How we handle spills shows how safe we are.

cards.title: Deal with it now, not later
cards.body: Never walk past a spill. The moment you spot one, take ownership. Warn anyone nearby, put out a wet floor sign, then clean it up properly. Absorb or mop the liquid and make sure the floor is actually dry. A damp floor is still a slip risk.

items.title: Sign it
items.text: Warn people nearby and put out a sign.

items.title: Clean it
items.text: Absorb or mop it up properly.

items.title: Dry it
items.text: Check the floor is completely dry.

cards.title: Make the sign mean something
cards.body: Leave the sign in place until the floor is completely dry, then take it away. A sign left out permanently just gets ignored, so it needs to mean something.

left.title: Do
items: Leave it out until the floor is dry

right.title: Do not
items: Remove it while the floor is damp

cards.title: Not every spill is the same
cards.body: Use the right method and equipment for what has been spilled. Water and drinks are one thing, but oil, grease or broken glass need extra care and the correct clean-up.

items.title: Oil and grease
items.text: Extra care and the correct clean-up.

items.title: Broken glass
items.text: Extra care and the correct clean-up.

cards.title: When it keeps coming back
cards.body: Once it is safe, mention recurring problems to your manager. If the same spot is always wet, we need to fix the cause, not just keep mopping.

cards.title: Remember
cards.body:
- Deal with a spill now and never walk past it
- Spot it, sign it, clean it, dry it
- A damp floor is still a slip risk
- Leave the sign until the floor is dry, then remove it
- Report any spot that keeps getting wet

cards.q: A wet patch you can barely see can still cause a serious slip.
cards.why: A wet patch you can barely see can put a guest or colleague flat on their back in an instant.

cards.q: What is the golden rule when you spot a spillage?
options: Tell the cleaner at the end of the shift
Deal with it now, not later
Wait until it is quiet, then clean it
Stand over it until a manager comes
cards.why: Deal with it now and never walk past it. The moment you spot a spill, take ownership.

cards.q: While cleaning a spill you should…
options: Say nothing, so guests do not worry
Turn the lights down to keep things calm
Put out a wet floor sign and warn people
Ask a guest to step round it
cards.why: Warn anyone nearby and put out a wet floor sign so people know the floor is wet.

cards.q: A damp floor is fine to walk on because it is not fully wet.
cards.why: A damp floor is still a slip risk. Make sure the floor is actually dry.

cards.q: When should you remove the wet floor sign?
options: At the end of the day
When you have finished mopping
When the floor is completely dry
When the next person asks
cards.why: Leave the sign until the floor is completely dry. Then take it away so it still means something.

cards.q: Oil, grease or broken glass need extra care and the correct clean-up.
cards.why: Water and drinks are one thing, but oil, grease and broken glass need the right method and equipment.

cards.q: If the same spot is always wet, what should you do beyond mopping?
options: Keep mopping it each time it happens
Report it so the cause can be fixed
Leave a sign out there permanently
Put a mat down and say nothing
cards.why: If the same spot is always wet, we need to fix the cause. Tell your manager rather than just mopping.

cards.q: Leaving wet floor signs out permanently means they get ignored.
cards.why: A sign left out permanently just gets ignored, so it needs to mean something.

cards.q: The four steps for a spill are: spot it, sign it, clean it, and…
options: Leave it
Photograph it
Report it to a guest
Dry it
cards.why: Spot it, sign it, clean it, dry it. The floor must be actually dry, not just mopped.

cards.q: Dealing with a spill is only the cleaner's responsibility.
cards.why: The moment you spot a spillage, take ownership. It is everyone's job in every department.
